history.content: What differentiates index funds and ETFs?

Index funds and ETFs are similar in that they both track an index, but there are differences between them. The differences between Index Funds and ETFs can be attributed to four main factors: expense ratio, tracking error, demand and supply, and liquidity. 
1. Expense Ratio: This is the fee charged by the fund for managing the portfolio. Since different funds have different expense ratios, this can lead to a difference in performance.
2. Tracking Error: This refers to the small percentage of error between the actual index composition and the fund composition. This discrepancy can result in a difference in values.
3. Demand and Supply: ETFs are traded on stock exchanges like stocks, and their prices can fluctuate based on demand and supply. If the general feeling is that the index is rising, it could lead to an increase in the price of the ETF. On the other hand, index funds remain the same for the day and are less liquid.
4. Liquidity: ETFs generally offer greater liquidity than index funds, allowing for easier buying and selling throughout the trading day.
Regarding which one to buy, it depends on other factors such as how easy it is to buy ETFs, whether you already hold a Demat account and have access to brokers, and whether you are comfortable with the less liquid nature of index funds.
In some cases, the index fund and ETF may not have the same benchmark and fees, making comparisons more complex. It is recommended to examine this question on a case-by-case basis, comparing the actual funds and ETFs in question, as returns are publicly available and can be checked directly.
Lastly, index funds are inherently diversified across their index, whereas ETFs allow for smaller initial purchases, enabling a more flexible mix of sectors.
How does the liquidity of ETFs compare to that of index funds?

ETFs generally offer greater liquidity than index funds. This is because ETFs are traded on stock exchanges throughout the trading day, allowing for buying and selling at any time during market hours. In contrast, index funds are typically only priced and traded once per day, after the close of the market. As a result, investors looking to buy or sell index funds may need to wait until the end of the trading day to complete their transactions. Additionally, the liquidity of ETFs can also be affected by demand and supply factors, as well as the underlying assets being traded.
I believe index funds offered more liquidity options.

It seems there might be a misunderstanding. Generally, ETFs are considered to offer greater liquidity than index funds due to their ability to be traded throughout the day on stock exchanges. Index funds, on the other hand, are typically only priced and traded once per day, after the close of the market. However, the liquidity of both types of investments can depend on various factors, including the specific fund or ETF, the assets it holds, and market conditions.

evidence.text: Bond ETFs are just another way to buy a bond mutual fund.  An ETF lets you trade mutual fund shares the way you trade stocks, in small share-size increments.  The content of this answer applies equally to both stock and bond funds. If you are intending to buy and hold these securities, your main concerns should be purchase fees and expense ratios.  Different brokerages will charge you different amounts to purchase these securities.  Some brokerages have their own mutual funds for which they charge no trading fees, but they charge trading fees for ETFs.  Brokerage A will let you buy Brokerage A's mutual funds for no trading fee but will charge a fee if you purchase Brokerage B's mutual fund in your Brokerage A account. Some brokerages have multiple classes of the same mutual fund.  For example, Vanguard for many of its mutual funds has an Investor class (minimum $3,000 initial investment), Admiral class (minimum $10,000 initial investment), and an ETF (share price as initial

An index fund is inherently diversified across its index -- no one stock will either make or break the results. In that case it's a matter of picking the index(es) you want to put the money into. ETFs do permit smaller initial purchases, which would let you do a reasonable mix of sectors. (That seems to be the one advantage of ETFs over traditional funds...?)

Choosing your broker and your funds may end up being more important than choosing the form of mutual fund versus ETF.  Some brokers charge very high purchase/redemption fees for mutual funds.  Many brokers have no ETFs that they will trade for free.  Between funds, index funds are passively managed and are just designed to track a certain index; they have lower ERs.  Actively managed funds are run by managers who try to beat the market; they have higher ERs and tend to actually fall below the performance of index funds, a double whammy. See also Vanguard's explanation of mutual funds vs. ETFs at Vanguard. See also Investopedia's explanation of mutual funds vs. ETFs in general.
